content: Every year, approximately one million children and young adolescents develop tuberculosis (TB), and around 226,000 of these children die from the disease. The Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra) is a molecular diagnostic test recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for the rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and rifampicin resistance. This test is particularly valuable because it provides results quickly and simultaneously identifies TB and resistance to rifampicin, a key first-line anti-TB drug. A previous Cochrane Review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra for TB and rifampicin resistance in children. The current review updates the evidence specifically for Xpert Ultra, focusing on its diagnostic performance in children suspected of having TB. This updated review also contributed to the 2022 WHO guidelines on managing TB in children and adolescents. The primary objective of this review was to assess the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert Ultra for detecting pulmonary TB, tuberculous meningitis, lymph node TB, and rifampicin resistance in children presumed to have TB. Secondary objectives included exploring potential sources of variability in diagnostic accuracy, such as age, comorbidities (e.g., HIV, severe pneumonia, severe malnutrition), and specimen type. The review also aimed to summarize the frequency of trace results, which indicate the detection of very low levels of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA. The review included cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, and randomized trials that evaluated Xpert Ultra in children under 15 years of age, both HIV-positive and HIV-negative. Studies were included if they assessed specimens such as sputum, gastric aspirate, stool, nasopharyngeal aspirate (for pulmonary TB), cerebrospinal fluid (for tuberculous meningitis), or fine needle aspirate/surgical biopsy tissue (for lymph node TB). The reference standards for TB detection were microbiological culture or a composite reference standard, while for rifampicin resistance, drug susceptibility testing or MTBDRplus was used. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using the QUADAS-2 tool to evaluate the risk of bias. Sensitivity and specificity estimates were calculated using a bivariate model, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review identified 14 studies, including 11 new studies since the previous review. For pulmonary TB detection, data from 25,937 participants across 335 datasets were analyzed. However, no studies evaluated Xpert Ultra for tuberculous meningitis or lymph node TB. Three studies assessed Xpert Ultra for rifampicin resistance. Most studies (71%) were conducted in countries with a high TB burden, as classified by WHO. Overall, the risk of bias was low. For pulmonary TB detection: Sputum (5 studies): Xpert Ultra had a sensitivity of 75.3% (95% CI: 64.3–83.8) and a specificity of 97.1% (95% CI: 94.7–98.5), with high-certainty evidence. Gastric aspirate (7 studies): Sensitivity was 70.4% (95% CI: 53.9–82.9) and specificity was 94.1% (95% CI: 84.8–97.8), with moderate-certainty evidence. Stool (6 studies): Sensitivity was 56.1% (95% CI: 39.1–71.7) and specificity was 98.0% (95% CI: 93.3–99.4), with moderateto high-certainty evidence. Nasopharyngeal aspirate (4 studies): Sensitivity was 43.7% (95% CI: 26.7–62.2) and specificity was 97.5% (95% CI: 93.6–99.0), with very lowto high-certainty evidence. Xpert Ultra's sensitivity was generally lower when compared to a composite reference standard rather than culture, except for nasopharyngeal aspirates. Specificity was similar across both reference standards. To illustrate the results: In a population of 1,000 children where 100 have pulmonary TB confirmed by sputum culture: 101 children would test positive with Xpert Ultra, but 26 of these would not have TB (false positives). 899 children would test negative, but 25 of these would actually have TB (false negatives). For gastric aspirate, stool, and nasopharyngeal aspirate, similar patterns of false positives and false negatives were observed, with sensitivity and specificity varying by specimen type. For rifampicin resistance detection: Xpert Ultra demonstrated a sensitivity of 100% (3 studies, 3 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and a specificity ranging from 97% to 100% (3 studies, 128 participants; low-certainty evidence). Trace results, which indicate very low levels of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA, were common in children. Despite this, Xpert Ultra maintained high specificity in pediatric populations. In conclusion, Xpert Ultra's sensitivity for TB detection varied by specimen type, with sputum showing the highest sensitivity, followed by gastric aspirate and stool, while nasopharyngeal aspirate had the lowest sensitivity. Specificity was consistently high across all specimen types and reference standards. Although Xpert Ultra was accurate for detecting rifampicin resistance, the evidence was based on a very small number of studies, and caution is warranted when interpreting these findings. Overall, the results support the use of Xpert Ultra as an initial rapid molecular diagnostic tool for evaluating TB in children.
